=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: "He doesn't want to settle": Trump says he does not want to deal with Zelenskyy ===

[Source 1 — www.pravda.com.ua] (URL: https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2026/10/16/8058255/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
"He doesn't want to settle": Trump says he does not want to deal with Zelenskyy

In an interview with Newsmax, US President Donald Trump accuses Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being unwilling to negotiate with Moscow, criticises Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and describes Russia's failed 2022 advance on Kyiv as partly down to the weather.

Actual Article Body:
Долучайтеся до клубу УП!

US President Donald Trump has said he does not want to deal with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy because he believes Zelenskyy is unwilling to reach an agreement with Russia. Trump also described Ukraine's repelling of the Russian advance on the city of Kyiv at the beginning of the full-scale invasion as a matter of luck.

Source: Trump in an interview with Newsmax

Details: Trump said Zelenskyy was not the person we should be dealing with. He claimed that any peace deal with Russia, if one is reached, would be concluded without Ukraine's current leader.

"He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't. No, I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," the US president said.

Trump also claimed that the root cause of the war was Barack Obama's presidency, during which Ukraine was supposedly made to "give up Crimea". The US president described the temporarily occupied peninsula as the "most beautiful piece of land", surrounded by ocean on all sides.

Quote: "Crimea is the most valuable part, by far, of Ukraine. You know what I'm talking about. Four sides of ocean. Most beautiful piece of land. I'm a real estate developer. I know good land."

Details: In the interview, Trump described strikes by Ukraine's defence forces on Russian oil refineries as a disgrace.

Quote: "I want Zelenskyy to stop, and I want Putin… Now, if you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace."

Details: Trump also attributed the failure of Russia's blitzkrieg against Kyiv in 2022 to the weather.

Quote: "Then it was supposed to be a very quick war. And if you remember the tanks going up the highway right into Kyiv, had the general, who was obviously not a very good general, not made a right turn into farmland, which was soaked and soaking wet from the heaviest rain in 10 years, they say. He went right up into the mud, and it was like quicksand, and those tanks, so they [the Ukrainians] got… I don't know if you call it lucky or not lucky, frankly."

Details: In Trump's view, Zelenskyy should make concessions to Putin because Moscow has a much larger pool of manpower to draw on in a war of attrition.

"But Russia is a massive country. Russia has millions of people," he said.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump’s recent diesel agreement with Russia has sparked backlash from Ukraine and a bipartisan group of senators. Under the agreement, Russia has pledged to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets to ease rising fuel prices. As lawmakers press the administration to withdraw from the agreement, Nigeria could emerge as a potential additional diesel supplier if the Trump administration seeks other fuel sources. Nigeria remains Africa’s top crude oil producer, the largest African supplier of crude oil to the United States, and has significantly ramped up its refining capacity, becoming an important supplier of diesel to global markets.

Historically, the U.S. and Nigeria have a complex, strategic partnership based on deep economic and security cooperation with periods of diplomatic friction. While the foundation for expanding bilateral energy cooperation already exists, Nigeria’s capacity to supply additional diesel to the U.S. and international markets faces multiple challenges, such as refining constraints, rising domestic fuel demand, and declining crude oil production.

DOJ indictments target alleged non-citizen voter fraud in Minnesota as Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss the charges. McCotter reveals that federal prosecutors have charged 50 individuals with voting crimes over the past month. The DOJ is also appealing a Florida federal judge's ruling that declared a federal law banning non-citizen voting unconstitutional.

The Trump administration is being sued over its efforts to collect and analyze sensitive voter data from across the country.

The complaint, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, alleges the Department of Homeland Security has obtained voter files from at least 47 states and handled the data in a way that violates federal law.

DHS' secretive probe of the voter data, which includes a policy to combine it with commercial datasets, ignores federal safeguards and the privacy rights of millions of Americans, the lawsuit says.

The case was brought by the League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and the League of United Latin American Citizens and is the latest legal challenge to President Donald Trump's efforts to combat noncitizen voting.

STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS

The Trump administration is being sued over its efforts to collect and analyze sensitive voter data from across the country. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images)

The president has purported repeatedly argued that noncitizen voting poses a serious threat to election integrity, although studies and prosecutions have found documented instances of noncitizens casting ballots to be rare.

The administration has repeatedly sought a greater federal role in voter eligibility and election administration, areas traditionally overseen primarily by states under the Constitution and federal law.

Federal courts have repeatedly rejected administration efforts to compel states to turn over voter information.

DHS' secretive probe of the voter data, which includes a policy to combine it with commercial datasets, ignores federal safeguards and the privacy rights of millions of Americans, the lawsuit says. (Joseph Prezioso/AFP/Getty Images)

The new lawsuit alleges the administration has obtained and processed voter records from at least 47 states, even though officials in 30 states have previously refused federal demands to turn over voter information.

The complaint urges the court to declare the administration's collection of voter data illegal, block DHS' policy and order the agency to delete and stop using the voter information it has already obtained.

The lawsuit comes less than three weeks before Election Day, and the administration continues to pressure states, alleging they are not doing enough to purge noncitizens from their voter rolls.

TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN IN ELECTION INTEGRITY FIGHT AS STATES GAIN NEW VOTER ROLL TOOL

The president has repeatedly argued that noncitizen voting poses a serious threat to election integrity, although documented instances of noncitizens casting ballots are rare. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The administration sued California election officials on Thursday, arguing they failed to act quickly enough to review names the federal government identified as "likely" noncitizens. The Justice Department asked a judge to block the state from counting mail-in ballots from those individuals unless their eligibility can be confirmed.

The California secretary of state's office said it was given only 48 hours to review roughly 20,000 names and said the federal government had not provided the underlying evidence or methodology supporting its claims.

The Justice Department's lawsuit, however, says U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services conducted a "multiagency and multilevel review" and determined with "high confidence" that roughly 20,000 people on California's voter rolls were likely noncitizens.

DHS did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.
